methods.label: radial annuli
methods.theory: Groups shapes by their distance from the mean shape alone, splitting the radius into k concentric shells with 1-D k-means so boundaries follow gaps in the distribution. Clusters are numbered inner to outer.
methods.use_when: You want to stratify an ensemble by how far it departs from the mean — the typical core, the intermediate band, the outliers — rather than find modes in a scatter.
methods.caveat: Uses only the radius, so two shapes that differ in kind but sit at the same distance land in the same shell. That is a deliberate trade: the radius is the coordinate the log map preserves exactly, so this is the one grouping here that involves no flattening distortion at all.

methods.label: agglomerative · average
methods.theory: Hierarchical agglomerative clustering. Starts with every shape in its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two whose average pairwise distance is smallest, then cuts the resulting tree to leave k groups.
methods.use_when: A sensible default. Makes no assumption about cluster shape or size and is stable against a few outliers.
methods.caveat: Uses pairwise separation, which the flattening distorts away from the mean — so read the result as local structure relative to the mean, not as a global statement about the manifold.

methods.label: agglomerative · ward
methods.theory: Agglomerative clustering that merges whichever pair increases total within-cluster variance the least — the hierarchical analogue of what k-means optimizes.
methods.use_when: You expect compact, roughly equal-sized groups and want crisper boundaries than average linkage gives.
methods.caveat: Actively prefers equal-sized clusters, so it will split one genuinely large population rather than report it. Minimizing variance is well defined on normal coordinates (a tangent space is Euclidean); it is less natural applied to raw geodesic distances as a feature.

methods.label: agglomerative · complete
methods.theory: Agglomerative clustering that merges the pair whose furthest two members are closest, so every cluster has a bounded diameter.
methods.use_when: You want tight, compact clusters and would rather over-split than chain two groups together.
methods.caveat: Driven by the single worst pair, so one outlier can hold a merge back indefinitely.

methods.label: agglomerative · single
methods.theory: Agglomerative clustering that merges the pair whose closest two members are nearest — a nearest-neighbour chain.
methods.use_when: Clusters are elongated or filamentary rather than blobs, e.g. a family of shapes deforming continuously along a path.
methods.caveat: Prone to chaining: a thin bridge of intermediate shapes will fuse two otherwise distinct populations into one.

methods.label: k-means
methods.theory: Places k centroids and alternates between assigning each shape to its nearest centroid and recomputing the centroids, minimizing within-cluster squared distance.
methods.use_when: Large ensembles where the agglomerative methods' pairwise-distance matrix becomes expensive.
methods.caveat: Assumes isotropic, similarly-sized clusters. Centroids are arithmetic means in the chosen coordinates — legitimate in a tangent space, but note a centroid is a point in normal coordinates, not a Karcher mean of the shapes it covers. Seeded for reproducibility, though it can still settle in a local optimum.
